sets.title: Digestive physiology and metabolism past questions

questions.stem: The term 'metabolism':

options.label: A
options.text: refers to all the chemical reactions that occur in the body

options.label: B
options.text: includes the synthesis of complex molecules from simpler ones

options.label: C
options.text: includes the breakdown of complex molecules into simpler ones

questions.why: Metabolism encompasses all chemical reactions, including both anabolic (building) and catabolic (breaking down) pathways.

notes.A: True, but so are the others.
notes.B: True, but so are the others.
notes.C: True, but so are the others.
notes.D: True, but so are the others.

questions.stem: An example of absorption is the:

options.label: B
options.text: active transport of glucose into a villus

options.label: C
options.text: hydrolysis of a peptide into amino acids

options.label: D
options.text: release of secretin in the presence of HCl

questions.why: Absorption is the movement of nutrients (like glucose) from the gut lumen into the blood or lymph.

questions.stem: Chewing food aids digestion by:

options.label: B
options.text: increasing the surface area of the food

options.label: C
options.text: breaking up large protein molecules into peptides

questions.why: Chewing (mastication) mechanically breaks food into smaller pieces, increasing the surface area for enzymatic action.

questions.stem: A function of the small intestine is to:
questions.why: The small intestine is the primary site of nutrient absorption.

notes.C: Gut bacteria in the colon make vitamin K.

questions.stem: In the GI tract, the layer, responsible for absorption and secretion is:
questions.why: The mucosa is the innermost lining where epithelial cells handle absorption and secretion.

questions.stem: Most of the chemical and mechanical digestion is carried out within:
questions.why: The small intestine is the primary site for the chemical digestion of nutrients and the absorption of the resulting molecules.

questions.stem: The chyme movement and flow into the stomach is controlled by:

options.label: E
options.text: both the nervous system and various digestive system hormones

questions.why: Gastric motility is regulated by both the enteric nervous system (parasympathetic/sympathetic) and hormones (gastrin, secretin, CCK).

questions.stem: Gastrointestinal hormones:

options.label: A
options.text: are secreted by exocrine glands of the gut mucosa and affect metabolism

options.label: B
options.text: are secreted into the blood stream by specialized cells in the gut walls and modulate its motor and secretory activity

options.label: C
options.text: are secreted by the gastric walls and protect the gut mucosa from the effect of HCl and proteolytic enzymes

options.label: D
options.text: are situated in the epithelial intestinal cells (enterocytes) and control the cell metabolism of nutrients

options.label: E
options.text: are secreted by the gastric walls and colon and protect the gut mucosa from the effect of HCl and proteolytic and nucleic enzymes

questions.why: GI hormones (like gastrin, secretin, CCK) are secreted by enteroendocrine cells into the blood to regulate motility and secretion.

questions.stem: The gastrointestinal enzymes:

options.label: A
options.text: are situated in the epithelial intestinal cells (enterocytes) and control cell metabolism

options.label: B
options.text: are secreted into the blood stream by specialized cells in the gut walls and modulate its motor and secretory activity

options.label: C
options.text: are secreted by exocrine glands of the gut mucosa and break down nutrients

options.label: D
options.text: are secreted by the gastric walls and protect the gut mucosa from the effect of HCl and proteolytic enzymes

options.label: E
options.text: are secreted by the gastric walls into the small intestine and protect the gut mucosa from the effect of HCl, proteolytic and nucleic enzymes

questions.why: Digestive enzymes are exocrine secretions that break down macromolecules into absorbable units.

questions.stem: All are GIT hormones except:
questions.why: Erythropoietin is a hormone produced by the kidneys that stimulates red blood cell production, not a GI hormone.

questions.stem: The enzyme amylase is secreted by:
questions.why: Amylase is found in saliva (salivary amylase) and pancreatic juice (pancreatic amylase) to digest carbohydrates.

notes.A: The liver makes no amylase; the duodenum receives it.
notes.B: The duodenum does not secrete it.
notes.C: The liver does not secrete it.

questions.stem: The digestive enzyme, produced in the salivary glands and the pancreas is:
questions.why: Amylase is produced by both salivary glands and the pancreas to digest starch.

questions.stem: The humoral and pharmacological factors inhibiting salivary secretion are:
questions.why: Sympathetic activity (catecholamines, adrenergic agonists) inhibits salivation (causing dry mouth), as do anticholinergics.

questions.stem: Saliva:

options.label: A
options.text: from different salivary glands has a similar composition

options.label: B
options.text: contains enzymes essential for the digestion of proteins

options.label: C
options.text: has less than half the ionic calcium level of plasma

options.label: D
options.text: has more than twice the iodide level of plasma

questions.why: Saliva concentrates iodine, having levels much higher than plasma.

questions.stem: Swallowing is a reflex which:

options.label: A
options.text: has its reflex centres in the cervical segments of the spinal cord

options.label: B
options.text: is initiated by a voluntary act and includes inhibition of respiration

options.label: C
options.text: has its reflex centres in the thoracic segments of the spinal cord

options.label: D
options.text: is not dependent on intrinsic nerve networks in the oesophagus

options.label: E
options.text: is more effective when the person is lying down rather than when standing

questions.why: Swallowing begins voluntarily but becomes an involuntary reflex that momentarily inhibits breathing to prevent aspiration.

notes.A: The centre is in the medulla.

questions.stem: Secretion of saliva increases when:

options.label: B
options.text: the mouth is flushed with fluids with a pH of about 7

options.label: C
options.text: the subject thinks of unappetizing food

options.label: E
options.text: the saliva glands parasympathetic nerve supply is stimulated

questions.why: Parasympathetic stimulation is the primary driver of salivary secretion.

notes.B: Neutral fluid is a weak stimulus.

questions.stem: Muscle tone in the lower oesophagus is:

options.label: A
options.text: lower than tone in the middle oesophagus

options.label: B
options.text: a major factor in preventing heartburn

questions.why: The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) maintains tone to prevent gastric acid from refluxing into the esophagus.

questions.stem: Normal swallowing is dependant on the integrity of the:
questions.why: Swallowing relies heavily on the glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) cranial nerves.

questions.stem: Saliva is responsible for all except:

options.label: E
options.text: maintaining the oral pH at about 7.0

questions.why: Saliva does not contain proteases that completely digest proteins (only lingual lipase and amylase for fats/carbs).

questions.stem: Which of the following has the lowest pH?
questions.why: Gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid (HCl) and has a highly acidic pH of roughly 1.5 to 3.5.

questions.stem: When parietal cells are stimulated, they secrete:
questions.why: Parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor (essential for B12 absorption).

notes.C: HCO3- goes to the BLOOD (alkaline tide).
notes.D: Bicarbonate is not secreted into the lumen.
notes.E: These come from mucous and chief cells.

questions.stem: Secretion of HCl by the gastric parietal cells is needed for:
questions.why: The acidic environment converts inactive pepsinogen into active pepsin, the main proteolytic enzyme of the stomach.

questions.stem: Gastric acid secretion is decreased by:
questions.why: The vagus nerve stimulates gastric acid secretion. Therefore, vagal inhibition decreases it.

questions.stem: This keeps the chyme in the stomach until it reaches the right consistency to pass into the small intestine:
questions.why: The pyloric sphincter regulates the emptying of chyme from the stomach into the duodenum.

notes.A: Upper and lower oesophageal sphincters guard the oesophagus.

questions.stem: Parietal cells secrete:
questions.why: Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid (and intrinsic factor).

questions.stem: The cells at the base of fundic or oxyntic glands are:
questions.why: Chief cells (peptic cells) are located deep in the gastric glands and secrete pepsinogen.

questions.stem: Which enzymes are secreted with the gastric juice:

options.label: E
options.text: proteolytic, nucleolytic, lipolytic and amylolytic enzymes

questions.why: Gastric juice contains pepsinogen (protease precursor) and gastric lipase.

notes.B: Trypsinogen is pancreatic; maltase is brush border.

questions.stem: The humoral factors inhibiting gastric motility are:

options.label: B
options.text: GIP, catecholamines, secretin, somatostatin, cholecystokinin- pancreozimin

options.label: E
options.text: intestinal hormones, somatostatin, secretin and cholecystokinin- pancreozimin

questions.why: Enterogastrones (like secretin, CCK, GIP) and catecholamines inhibit gastric motility to slow emptying when the duodenum is busy.

questions.stem: The humoral factors stimulating gastric motility are:

options.label: A
options.text: catecholamines, secretin, gastric peptide, somatostatin, cholecystokinin- pancreozimin

options.label: D
options.text: GIP, VIP, somatostatin, secretin and cholecystokinin- pancreozimin

questions.why: Gastrin and motilin stimulate gastric smooth muscle contraction and motility.

questions.stem: The humoral factors that inhibit gastric secretion are:

options.label: A
options.text: gastrin, histamine, acetylcholine, cholecystokinin-pancreozymin, bombesin, motilin

questions.why: Enterogastrones (GIP, secretin, CCK, VIP) act as hormones to inhibit gastric acid and pepsinogen secretion.

questions.stem: Which humoral factors stimulate gastric secretion:

options.label: B
options.text: secretin, cholecystokinin-pancreozymin, histamine, acetylcholine, bombesin, motilin

questions.why: The three direct stimulants of parietal cells are gastrin (via CCK-B receptors), histamine (H2) and acetylcholine (M3). Secretin and somatostatin INHIBIT acid secretion.

questions.stem: The physiological effect of gastrin on gastric secretion is:

options.label: A
options.text: increased amount of gastric juice of high acidity and low proteolytic activity

options.label: B
options.text: increased amount of gastric juice of low acidity and high proteolytic activity

options.label: C
options.text: to decrease the amount of gastric juice

options.label: D
options.text: decreased amount of gastric juice of high acidity and low proteolytic activity

options.label: E
options.text: decreased amount of gastric juice of low acidity

questions.why: Gastrin stimulates parietal cells (acid) more than chief cells (pepsinogen), resulting in high acidity but relatively low proteolytic activity.

questions.stem: The physiological effect of histamine on gastric secretion is:

options.label: A
options.text: increased amount of gastric juice of high acidity and low proteolytic activity

options.label: B
options.text: to decrease the amount of the gastric juice

options.label: C
options.text: increased amount of gastric juice of low acidity and high proteolytic activity

options.label: D
options.text: increased amount of gastric juice of low acidity and low proteolytic activity

options.label: E
options.text: no change in the amount or acidity of gastric juice

questions.why: Histamine strongly stimulates acid secretion (via H2 receptors) but has little effect on pepsinogen.

questions.stem: The chief cells of the stomach glands secrete:
questions.why: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, a proteolytic enzyme precursor.

questions.stem: In the stomach:

options.label: B
options.text: pepsinogen is converted to pepsin by hydrochloric acid

options.label: C
options.text: ferrous iron is reduced to ferric iron by hydrochloric acid

options.label: D
options.text: acid secretion is inhibited by pentagastrin

options.label: E
options.text: there is a rise in the bacterial count after histamine H1 receptor blockade

questions.why: Pepsinogen requires the acidic environment provided by HCl to become active pepsin.

questions.stem: The gastric juice:

options.label: A
options.text: is secreted when the vagus nerves are stimulated

options.label: B
options.text: is secreted in vagotomized animals when food is chewed but not swallowed

options.label: C
options.text: activates the digestive enzymes secreted with saliva

options.label: D
options.text: digests the gastric mucosa because it is not protected by a pepsin inactivator

options.label: E
options.text: does not irritate the oesophageal mucosa if regurgitated from the stomach

questions.why: Vagal stimulation (parasympathetic) strongly promotes gastric acid and pepsinogen secretion.

questions.stem: The normally innervated stomach:

options.label: A
options.text: is stimulated to secrete gastric juice when food is chewed, even if it is not swallowed

options.label: B
options.text: secrete HCl when its H1- histamine receptors are blocked

options.label: C
options.text: increases gastric secretion when there are fear and depression

options.label: D
options.text: empties slower than the denervated stomach

options.label: E
options.text: is stimulated to secrete gastric juice by the hormone secretin

questions.why: The cephalic phase of gastric secretion is triggered by the sight, smell, or taste of food (even just chewing), mediated by the vagus nerve.

notes.D: Empties faster than the denervated stomach.

questions.stem: Secretion of gastric juice:

options.label: A
options.text: decreases when food stimulates mucosal cells in the pyloric region

options.label: B
options.text: is associated with a decrease in the pH of venous blood draining the stomach

options.label: C
options.text: in response to food is increased after vagotomy

options.label: E
options.text: is essential for absorption of vitamin B12

questions.why: Gastric juice contains intrinsic factor, which is essential for Vitamin B12 absorption in the ileum.

questions.stem: Peptic ulcer pain is typically relieved by:

options.label: A
options.text: raising the pH of the fluid bathing the ulcer and a drug blocking the gastric proton pump

options.label: D
options.text: a drug which interferes with the action of acetylcholinesterase

options.label: E
options.text: a drug which stimulates the gastric proton pump

questions.why: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) decrease acid secretion, raising the pH and allowing the ulcer to heal.

questions.stem: Gastric:

options.label: A
options.text: acid secretion in response to a lowered blood sugar is mediated by the hormone gastrin

options.label: B
options.text: emptying is facilitated by sympathetic nerve activity

options.label: C
options.text: acid secretion increases when histamine H2, muscarinic M1 or gastrin receptors are activated

options.label: D
options.text: acid secretion is inhibited by the presence of food in the duodenum

questions.why: Gastric acid secretion is stimulated by histamine (H2), ACh (M3/M1), and gastrin. It is inhibited by enterogastrones when food (especially fat/acid) enters the duodenum.

questions.stem: Which of the following are incorrectly paired:
questions.why: Renin is an enzyme produced by the kidneys to regulate blood pressure. The milk-coagulating enzyme in the stomach is rennin (or chymosin).

questions.stem: Secretion of the intrinsic factor of Castle occurs in:
questions.why: Intrinsic factor is secreted by parietal cells.

questions.stem: Gastrin secretion is increased by:

options.label: A
options.text: acid in the lumen of stomach

questions.why: Vagal stimulation (parasympathetic) stimulates G cells to release gastrin.

questions.stem: The gastrin is secreted in the:
questions.why: Gastrin is primarily secreted by G cells located in the gastric antrum.

questions.stem: The motor activity of the stomach includes:
questions.why: The stomach exhibits receptive relaxation (to accommodate food), peristalsis (to mix and grind), and migrating motor complexes during fasting.

questions.stem: In the stomach:

options.label: B
options.text: pepsinogen is converted into pepsin under the influence of HCl

options.label: C
options.text: Fe2+ is oxidised to Fe3+ under the influence of HCl

options.label: D
options.text: HCl secretion is suppressed by pentagastrin

options.label: E
options.text: the bacterial count increases after applying H1-receptor blockers

questions.why: HCl is required to activate pepsinogen into pepsin.

notes.C: Acid helps REDUCE Fe3+ to Fe2+.

questions.stem: The lowest pH is characteristic of the:
questions.why: Gastric juice has the lowest pH (most acidic).

questions.stem: Release of which one of the following increases the pH of duodenal contents?
questions.why: Secretin stimulates the pancreas to release a bicarbonate-rich fluid, which neutralizes the acidic chyme and raises the pH in the duodenum.

questions.stem: In the duodenum in response to acidic chyme is released:
questions.why: Acidic chyme entering the duodenum stimulates S cells to release secretin.

notes.A: CCK is released by fat and protein.
notes.E: An enzyme, not released by acid.

questions.stem: Which enzymes are secreted with the pancreatic juice:

options.label: B
options.text: proteolytic: trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, elastase, carboxypeptidase, etc.

questions.why: Pancreatic juice is rich in all classes of digestive enzymes: lipolytic, proteolytic, amylolytic, and nucleolytic.

questions.stem: Which of the bile components are important for digestion:
questions.why: Bile salts are the primary components essential for emulsifying fats to aid digestion.

questions.stem: The humoral factors that stimulate the formation and secretion of bile are:

options.label: C
options.text: secretin, gastrin, cholecystokinin- pancreozimin, bile salts

questions.why: Secretin stimulates bile duct secretion (bicarbonate), while CCK stimulates gallbladder contraction. Bile salts stimulate their own secretion via enterohepatic circulation.

questions.stem: The humoral factors that inhibit the formation and secretion of bile are:

options.label: E
options.text: insulin, glucagon, catecholamines, growth hormone, glucocorticoids, thyroid hormones

questions.why: Sympathetic stimulation (catecholamines) generally inhibits bile secretion and gallbladder contraction.

questions.stem: The humoral factors that stimulate the secretion of pancreatic juice are:

options.label: C
options.text: secretin, cholecystokinin- pancreozimin, gastrin, serotonin,VIP, insulin

options.label: E
options.text: glucagon, insulin, catecholamines, growth hormone, glucocorticoids, thyroid hormones

questions.why: Secretin (bicarbonate) and CCK (enzymes) are the primary stimulants of pancreatic exocrine secretion.

questions.stem: As far as bile is considered:

options.label: A
options.text: contains enzymes required for the digestion of fat

options.label: C
options.text: bile salts make cholesterol more water- soluble

options.label: E
options.text: becomes more alkaline during storage in the gallbladder

questions.why: Bile salts act as detergents to emulsify fats and cholesterol, making them soluble in the aqueous chyme.

questions.stem: Pancreatic secretion:

options.label: A
options.text: in response to vagal stimulation is copious, rich in bicarbonate but poor in enzymes

options.label: B
options.text: in response to acid in the duodenum is scanty but rich in enzymes

options.label: C
options.text: in response to secretin secretion is low in bicarbonate

options.label: D
options.text: contains enzymes that digest neutral fat to glycerol and fatty acids

options.label: E
options.text: contains enzymes that convert disaccharides to monosaccharides

questions.why: Pancreatic lipase digests neutral fats (triglycerides) into fatty acids and monoglycerides/glycerol.

notes.B: Acid gives a copious, bicarbonate-rich juice.

questions.stem: The liver is the principal site for:
questions.why: The liver synthesizes most plasma proteins, most notably albumin.

notes.D: Vitamin C is not stored mainly there.

questions.stem: The passage of acidic gastric contents to the duodenum may cause:

options.label: A
options.text: copious secretion of pancreatic juice rich in bicarbonate

options.label: D
options.text: contraction of the sphincter of Oddi

questions.why: Acid in the duodenum stimulates secretin release, leading to a bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion to neutralize the acid.

questions.stem: Bile salts:

options.label: A
options.text: derived from cholesterol, are the only constituents of bile necessary for digestion

options.label: B
options.text: have a characteristic molecule, being water-soluble

options.label: C
options.text: are reabsorbed mainly in the upper small intestine

questions.why: Bile salts are synthesized from cholesterol and are the essential component of bile for fat emulsification and digestion.

questions.stem: The cells of the liver:

options.label: A
options.text: help to maintain the normal blood glucose level

options.label: B
options.text: deaminate amino acids to form NH4+ which is excreted as ammonium salts in the urine

options.label: D
options.text: manufacture most of the immune globulins

options.label: E
options.text: activate steroid hormones manufactured in the gonads

questions.why: The liver plays a critical role in glucose homeostasis (glycogenesis, glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis).

questions.stem: Urobilinogen is:

options.label: A
options.text: a mixture of colourless compounds also known as stercobilinogen

options.label: B
options.text: formed in the reticuloendothelial system from bilirubin

questions.why: Urobilinogen is formed by bacterial action in the gut. Some is excreted in feces, and some is reabsorbed into the blood and excreted in urine.

questions.stem: Lack of pancreatic juice in the duodenum may lead to:

options.label: A
options.text: the presence of undigested meat fibres in the stools

options.label: B
options.text: an increase in the fat content of the faeces

options.label: C
options.text: a decrease in the fat of the faeces

options.label: D
options.text: a high prothrombin level in blood

questions.why: Without pancreatic enzymes, proteins and fats cannot be fully digested, leading to steatorrhea (fat in stool) and creatorrhea (undigested meat fibers).

questions.stem: Which of the following has the highest pH:
questions.why: Pancreatic juice is rich in bicarbonate and is highly alkaline (pH ~8.0-8.3), making it have the highest pH.

questions.stem: Secretin is released by:
questions.why: Acidic chyme entering the duodenum stimulates S cells to secrete secretin.

questions.stem: Choleretica are substances, which:

options.label: B
options.text: stimulate the secretion of bile by the liver

options.label: D
options.text: suppress the secretion of bile by the liver

questions.why: Choleretics stimulate bile secretion by the liver.

questions.stem: Enterohepatic circle refers to:
questions.why: The enterohepatic circulation is the recycling of bile salts from the ileum back to the liver.

notes.A: Amino acids are not recycled via bile.
notes.B: Fats are not recycled via bile.
notes.C: Carbohydrates are not recycled via bile.

questions.stem: Tripsinogen is converted into tripsin under the influence of:
questions.why: Enterokinase (enteropeptidase) from the duodenal mucosa converts trypsinogen to active trypsin.

notes.B: Iron salts do not activate trypsinogen.
notes.D: Gastrin stimulates acid, not trypsin activation.
notes.E: ACh stimulates secretion but does not activate trypsinogen.

questions.stem: Which are the bile components of basic significance for digestion:
questions.why: Bile salts are essential for fat emulsification.

questions.stem: Calcium absorption is facilitated by:
questions.why: Active Vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol) stimulates the synthesis of calbindin, which facilitates calcium absorption in the gut.

questions.stem: Fat absorption occurs mainly in the:
questions.why: Fat digestion and absorption primarily begin in the duodenum, where bile and pancreatic lipase are released.

notes.C: Bile salts, not fat, are absorbed there.
notes.D: Fat is gone by the caecum.
notes.E: Fat is gone by the colon.

questions.stem: The movements of the small intestine are:
questions.why: The small intestine exhibits both mixing (segmentation) contractions and propulsive (peristaltic) contractions.

questions.stem: Where the protein hydrolysis occurs:
questions.why: Protein digestion begins in the stomach (pepsin) and is completed in the small intestine (pancreatic proteases).

questions.stem: After a fatty meal is taken, most of the fat would be:

options.label: A
options.text: absorbed in the portal circulation and transported to the liver

options.label: B
options.text: absorbed in the portal vein and transported in the hepatic artery

options.label: C
options.text: absorbed as chylomicrons in the lymphatic system

options.label: D
options.text: absorbed as triglycerides into the portal vein and bypasses the liver

questions.why: Long-chain fatty acids are packaged into chylomicrons, which enter the lacteals (lymphatic system) rather than the portal blood.

notes.A: Short-chain fats go to the portal blood; most go to lymph.
notes.B: The hepatic artery is not involved.
notes.D: Not as triglycerides into the portal vein.

questions.stem: For fat digestion:

options.label: A
options.text: bile salts are the most efficient emulsifiers

options.label: B
options.text: gastric lipase is the most important

options.label: C
options.text: pancreatic lipase in the duodenum is needed

questions.why: Pancreatic lipase is the primary enzyme responsible for the hydrolysis of triglycerides into fatty acids and monoglycerides.

notes.A: They help, but lipase is indispensable.
notes.E: There is no receptor; products diffuse in.

questions.stem: In the small intestine, glucose is absorbed:

options.label: B
options.text: by secondary active transport (coupled to Na+ transport)

questions.why: Glucose absorption in the intestine uses SGLT1, a sodium-glucose linked transporter (secondary active transport).

questions.stem: After ingestion of a meal:

options.label: A
options.text: digestion of fat and carbohydrate begins in the mouth while protein digestion begins in the stomach

options.label: B
options.text: carbohydrates are digested in the stomach and proteins in the mouth

options.label: C
options.text: proteins are digested in the mouth and fats and carbohydrates in the stomach

options.label: D
options.text: most fluid and electrolytes are absorbed in the large bowel

options.label: E
options.text: composition of the food has no effect on transit time through the bowel

questions.why: Salivary amylase (carbs) and lingual lipase (fat) begin digestion in the mouth, while pepsin (protein) begins in the stomach.

notes.D: Most is absorbed in the SMALL intestine.

questions.stem: Calcium uptake in the intestine:

options.label: B
options.text: requires a carrier protein on the mucosal side

options.label: D
options.text: is less than 10% of dietary intake

questions.why: Active calcium absorption requires a calcium-binding carrier protein (calbindin) on the mucosal side of the enterocyte.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a water soluble vitamin?
questions.why: Vitamin B complex (and Vitamin C) are water-soluble. Vitamins A, D, E, and K are fat-soluble.

questions.stem: The function of the ileum is to:

options.label: B
options.text: absorb vitamin B12 and bile salts

questions.why: The terminal ileum is uniquely responsible for the absorption of vitamin B12 (with intrinsic factor) and the reabsorption of bile salts.

questions.stem: The enzymes, secreted with the intestinal juice are:

options.label: A
options.text: exopeptidases, lipase, maltase, nucleic (nuclease, nucleotidases, nucleosidases)

options.label: B
options.text: endo- and exopeptidases, esterase and amylolytic enzymes

options.label: D
options.text: aminopeptidase, dipeptidase, nuclease, somatostatin, secretin, cholecystokinin- pancreozimin

questions.why: Intestinal juice (succus entericus) contains enzymes like aminopeptidase, dipeptidase, nuclease, and lipase for final digestion.

questions.stem: The humoral factors that stimulate intestinal motility are:

options.label: C
options.text: cholecystokinin-pancreozymin, motilin, gastrin, substance P and serotonin

questions.why: Several gut hormones including CCK, VIP, and substance P stimulate intestinal motility.

questions.stem: The carbohydrates are absorbed as:
questions.why: Carbohydrates must be broken down into simple monosaccharides (like glucose, fructose, galactose) to be absorbed.

questions.stem: Defaecation is a reflex action:

options.label: A
options.text: that is coordinated by reflex centres in the sacral cord

options.label: B
options.text: whose afferent limb carries impulses from stretch receptors in the colon

options.label: C
options.text: whose efferent limb travels mainly in sympathetic autonomic nerves

options.label: D
options.text: which is more likely to be initiated just before a meal than just after it

options.label: E
options.text: which can be involuntarily inhibited or facilitated

questions.why: The defecation reflex is coordinated by the sacral segments of the spinal cord (S2-S4).

questions.stem: Intestinal juice contain:

options.label: A
options.text: potassium in a concentration similar to that in extracellular fluid

options.label: B
options.text: enzymes that are released when the vagus nerve is inhibited

options.label: E
options.text: enzymes that suppress pancreatic proteolytic enzymes

questions.why: Intestinal juice contains disaccharidases (like maltase, sucrase, lactase) to break disaccharides into monosaccharides.

questions.stem: In the small intestine:

options.label: A
options.text: the enzyme concentration in intestinal juice is higher in the ileum than in the jejunum

options.label: B
options.text: vitamin B12 is absorbed mainly in the jejunum

options.label: C
options.text: water absorption is independent on the active absorption of sodium and glucose

options.label: D
options.text: absorption of calcium occurs mainly in the terminal ileum

options.label: E
options.text: glucose absorption is dependent on sodium absorption

questions.why: Glucose is absorbed via SGLT-1, which requires the co-transport of sodium ions.

questions.stem: Absorption of dietary fat:

options.label: A
options.text: can only occur after the neutral fat has been split into glycerol and fatty acids

options.label: B
options.text: does not depend on their size

options.label: C
options.text: is impaired when bile salt reabsorption is prevented by resection of the terminal ileum

options.label: D
options.text: is carried out by passive diffusion

options.label: E
options.text: is greatest in the lower parts of the small intestine

questions.why: Resection of the terminal ileum prevents bile salt reabsorption, leading to a depletion of the bile salt pool and impaired fat digestion/absorption.

notes.D: Partly; impaired bile is the key point.

questions.stem: Cholesterol:

options.label: A
options.text: can be absorbed from the gut by intestinal lymphatics following its incorporation into chylomicrons

options.label: B
options.text: can be synthesized in the spleen

options.label: C
options.text: in the diet comes mainly from vegetable sources

options.label: D
options.text: is eliminated from the body mainly by metabolic degradation

options.label: E
options.text: is a precursor of adrenal medulla hormones

questions.why: Dietary cholesterol is packaged into chylomicrons and absorbed via the lymphatics.

notes.D: As bile salts and cholesterol in bile.

questions.stem: Impaired intestinal absorption of:

options.label: A
options.text: iron occurs frequently following removal of most of the stomach

options.label: B
options.text: iodine leads to a reduction in size of the thyroid gland

options.label: C
options.text: water occurs in infants who cannot digest lipids

options.label: D
options.text: calcium is typical after removal of the colon

options.label: E
options.text: bile salts may occur following resection of the stomach

questions.why: Gastric acid is needed to reduce iron to its absorbable ferrous (Fe2+) form. Gastrectomy can lead to iron deficiency anemia.

notes.D: Calcium is absorbed in the small intestine.

questions.stem: Complications that may arise after total gastrectomy include:

options.label: A
options.text: depletion of vitamin B12 stores in the liver

options.label: B
options.text: malabsorption of fat due to rapid intestinal transit

options.label: C
options.text: impaired defaecation due to loss of the gastric reflex

questions.why: Gastrectomy removes intrinsic factor (causing B12 deficiency) and the gastric reservoir (causing rapid dumping and fat malabsorption).

questions.stem: Severe diarrhoea causes a decrease in:
questions.why: Diarrhoeal fluid is rich in K+ and HCO3-, so body potassium and ECF volume fall. The volume loss RAISES ADH and, through sympathetic activation, peripheral resistance.

questions.stem: Surgical removal of 90% of the small intestine may cause an increase in:

options.label: A
options.text: the fat content of the stools

questions.why: Massive resection causes malabsorption of fat (steatorrhoea), so stool fat RISES, while bone mineralization, ECF volume, haemoglobin and body weight all fall.

questions.stem: Constipation is a recognized consequence of:

options.label: B
options.text: abnormality of the autonomic nerve supply to the esophagus

options.label: C
options.text: a diet that leaves little unabsorbed residue in the gut

options.label: D
options.text: over-activity of the thyroid gland as in thyrotoxicosis

questions.why: A low-fiber diet (low residue) leads to constipation. Psychological stress can also alter bowel habits.

questions.stem: Absorption of glucose by intestinal mucosal cells:

options.label: A
options.text: relies on a carrier mechanism in the cell membrane

options.label: B
options.text: is blocked not by the same agents that block renal reabsorption of glucose

options.label: C
options.text: is enhanced by blockade of active sodium transport in the cells

options.label: D
options.text: takes place mainly in the ileum

options.label: E
options.text: does not involve the same carriers that are used for the absorption of galactose

questions.why: Glucose absorption requires the SGLT-1 carrier protein on the apical membrane.

questions.stem: Iron is absorbed in:
questions.why: Iron is primarily absorbed in the duodenum.

questions.stem: In infants, defecation often follows a meal. The cause of colonic contractions in this situation is:
questions.why: The gastrocolic reflex stimulates colonic motility in response to stomach distension after a meal.

questions.stem: Man is unable to digest:
questions.why: Humans lack the enzyme cellulase, so they cannot digest cellulose (dietary fiber).

questions.stem: Steatorrhoea may be caused by all factors except:
questions.why: Hemolytic jaundice is due to excessive red blood cell breakdown, not fat malabsorption.

questions.stem: In which of the following is absorption of water greatest:
questions.why: Most water absorption occurs in the small intestine, primarily the jejunum.

questions.stem: Vit. D is essential for normal:
questions.why: Active Vitamin D is essential for intestinal calcium absorption.

questions.stem: The mass movements are characteristic of the:
questions.why: Mass movements are powerful peristaltic waves that move contents through the colon (large intestine).

questions.stem: The proteins are resorbed in the form of:
questions.why: Proteins are absorbed as small peptides (di/tri-peptides) and free amino acids.

questions.stem: The carbohydrates are resorbed as:
questions.why: Carbohydrates must be broken down into simple monosaccharides to be absorbed by enterocytes.

questions.stem: The fats are resorbed as:

options.label: A
options.text: glicerol, free fatty acids and cholesterol

questions.why: Fats are absorbed as monoglycerides, free fatty acids, and cholesterol.

questions.stem: The secretion of K+ is in the:
questions.why: Potassium is primarily secreted into the colon (regulated by aldosterone).

questions.stem: The propulsive peristalsis of the small intestine:

options.label: C
options.text: results from smooth muscle contractions behind and in front of the zone of irritation

options.label: D
options.text: results from smooth muscles' contraction behind the zone of irritation and relaxation in front of it

options.label: E
options.text: results from smooth muscles relaxation along the small intestine

questions.why: Peristalsis involves contraction behind the bolus and relaxation ahead of it to push it forward.

questions.stem: Steatorrhea is caused by:

options.label: C
options.text: stoppage of bile flow into the duodenum

options.label: D
options.text: the breakdown and reabsorption of fats are disturbed

questions.why: Steatorrhea (fat in stool) is caused by impaired fat digestion or absorption, such as bile duct obstruction or intestinal disease.

questions.stem: The segment movements of the small intestine are carried out by:

options.label: C
options.text: ring like contraction, when the segment in front relaxes

questions.why: Segmentation (mixing) contractions are primarily driven by the circular smooth muscle layer.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements concerning energy storage in the body is true?

options.label: A
options.text: most is stored in the form of ATP

options.label: B
options.text: most is stored in the form of glucose

options.label: C
options.text: most is stored in the form of fat

options.label: D
options.text: most is stored in the form of protein

options.label: E
options.text: most is stored in the form of DNA

questions.why: Adipose tissue (fat) is the body's primary long-term energy storage form.

notes.D: Protein is structural; it is used only in starvation.
notes.E: DNA is not an energy store.

questions.stem: The main source of energy in a typical human diet is:
questions.why: Carbohydrates are the body's preferred and main source of energy.

notes.C: Nucleic acids are trivial as fuel.
notes.E: Fat is energy-dense but not the main dietary source.

questions.stem: Which of the following organs or tissues is most dependent upon a constant blood supply of glucose?
questions.why: The brain relies almost exclusively on glucose for energy and cannot store significant amounts, making it highly dependent on a constant supply.

notes.D: Muscle uses fat and its own glycogen.

questions.stem: The hormones regulating carbohydrate metabolism (synthesis, catabolism) are:

options.label: B
options.text: insulin, glucagon, catecholamines, growth hormone, glucocorticoids (ACTH), T3 and T4 (TTH)

questions.why: Insulin lowers blood sugar; glucagon, catecholamines, GH, cortisol, and thyroid hormones raise it.

questions.stem: The hormones that increase significantly the basic metabolic rate are:
questions.why: Thyroid hormones (T3, T4) are the primary regulators of BMR, but catecholamines and glucocorticoids also increase it.

questions.stem: Glucose enters the blood stream via:

options.label: C
options.text: enterocytes' absorption, liver glycogen catabolism, hepatocytes and kidneys gluconeogenesis, renal proximal tubule epitheliocytes

options.label: D
options.text: degradation of glycogen in the skeletal muscles

questions.why: Blood glucose is maintained by intestinal absorption, hepatic glycogenolysis, and renal/hepatic gluconeogenesis.

questions.stem: The basal metabolic rate is the energy consumption of the body under the following conditions:

options.label: A
options.text: adequate intake of vitamins regulating the intermediate processes of metabolism of the various substances

options.label: B
options.text: normal function of the endocrine glands

options.label: C
options.text: physical and psychic rest, 12 hours after the last meal in a room at a temperature of 20 - 22°C

questions.why: BMR is measured under strict conditions: awake, fully rested, fasting (12+ hrs), and in a thermoneutral environment.

questions.stem: Humoral factors taking part in the calcium/ phosphorus homeostasis are:

options.label: B
options.text: parathyroid hormone, thyrocalcitonin and vitamin D3

options.label: E
options.text: antidiuretic hormone, androgens and angiotensin II

questions.why: PTH, calcitonin, and active Vitamin D (calcitriol) are the primary regulators of calcium and phosphate balance.

notes.A: Thyroxine is not a calcium hormone.

questions.stem: The body requires amino acids to:
questions.why: Amino acids are the building blocks for synthesizing new proteins and replacing damaged ones.

notes.A: Haem and globin need more than amino acids.

questions.stem: Which of the following will catalyze the breakdown of starches?
questions.why: Amylase specifically hydrolyzes starch into smaller carbohydrates.

questions.stem: Which molecule represents the storage form of glucose in the liver?
questions.why: Glucose is stored as glycogen in the liver and skeletal muscle.

questions.stem: Appetite for food is increased:
questions.why: Cold environments increase metabolic demand, stimulating appetite.

questions.stem: The respiratory quotient (RQ):

options.label: A
options.text: is the volume of O2 consumed to the volume of CO2 produced ratio

options.label: B
options.text: depends essentially on the type of substrate being metabolized and is 1.0 when the substrate is glucose

options.label: C
options.text: is 1.0 in conditions of metabolic alcalosis

options.label: D
options.text: is between 0.9 and 1.0 in the second week of fasting

options.label: E
options.text: is above 0.8 if fats are mainly metabolized

questions.why: RQ = CO2 produced / O2 consumed. It is 1.0 for pure carbohydrate metabolism and ~0.7 for fat.

questions.stem: Oxygen consumption tends to increase when the:

options.label: A
options.text: concentration of oxygen in inspired air rises

options.label: C
options.text: body temperature rises and environmental temperature falls

questions.why: Shivering thermogenesis (due to falling environmental temperature) and fever (rising body temperature) both increase O2 consumption.

questions.stem: Brown fat is:

options.label: A
options.text: relatively more abundant in adults than in infants

options.label: B
options.text: richer in mitochondria than ordinary fat and has an extensive sympathetic innervation

options.label: C
options.text: produces less heat and more ATP than other tissues

options.label: D
options.text: stimulated to generate more heat when its parasympathetic nerve supply is stimulated

options.label: E
options.text: less important than shivering in neonatal thermoregulation

questions.why: Brown adipose tissue is rich in mitochondria (using uncoupling protein 1) and is heavily innervated by sympathetic nerves to generate heat (non-shivering thermogenesis).

questions.stem: Nitrogen balance:

options.label: A
options.text: is the relationship between the body's nitrogen intake and nitrogen loss

options.label: C
options.text: becomes more positive when dietary protein is decreased

options.label: D
options.text: becomes positive whenever a single essential amino acid is omitted from the diet

options.label: E
options.text: becomes less negative in the final stages of fatal starvation

questions.why: Nitrogen balance compares nitrogen intake (from protein) to nitrogen excretion.

questions.stem: The specific dynamic action of food:

options.label: A
options.text: is the decrease in metabolic rate that results from ingestion of food

options.label: B
options.text: persists for about an hour after a meal is ingested

options.label: C
options.text: is due to the additional energy expended in digesting and absorbing the food

options.label: D
options.text: results in about 30 per cent of the energy value of ingested protein being unavailable for other purposes

options.label: E
options.text: results in about 20 per cent of the energy value of ingested fat and carbohydrate being unavailable for other purposes

questions.why: The thermic effect of food (SDA) for protein is the highest, around 30%, because a lot of energy is used to deaminate and synthesize proteins.

notes.C: Due to metabolic processing, not digestion.
notes.E: Much less for fat and carbohydrate (about 5%).

questions.stem: One gram of:

options.label: A
options.text: carbohydrate, metabolized in the body, yields more energy when oxidized in a bomb calorimeter

options.label: B
options.text: fat, metabolized in the body, yields 10 per cent more energy than 1g of carbohydrate

options.label: C
options.text: protein, metabolized in the body, yields the same energy as when oxidized in a bomb calorimeter

options.label: D
options.text: carbohydrate, metabolized in the body, yields about the same energy as 1g of protein

options.label: E
options.text: protein per kg body weight is not the adequate daily protein intake for a sedentary adult

questions.why: Carbohydrates and proteins both yield approximately 4 kcal/g, while fats yield about 9 kcal/g.

questions.stem: Free (non-esterified) fatty acids in plasma:

options.label: A
options.text: are carried in plasma mainly inside chylomicrons

options.label: C
options.text: decrease when the level of blood adrenaline rises

options.label: D
options.text: cannot be used for energy by cardiac muscle

options.label: E
options.text: are never synthesized in adipose tissue

questions.why: Free fatty acids are hydrophobic and must be bound to albumin to travel in the aqueous plasma.

notes.A: They are released from lipoproteins and travel on albumin.
notes.D: The heart uses them a lot.

questions.stem: Fat stores in the adult:

options.label: A
options.text: make up less than 5 % of average body weight

options.label: B
options.text: Make up a smaller percentage of body weight in women than in men

options.label: C
options.text: release fatty acids when there is increased sympathetic nerve activity

options.label: D
options.text: release fatty acids when insulin is injected

options.label: E
options.text: enlarge by increasing the number of adipocytes they contain

questions.why: Sympathetic stimulation (via beta-3 receptors) stimulates lipolysis in adipose tissue.

questions.stem: Metabolic rate can be estimated from measurements of:

options.label: B
options.text: the calorific value of the food consumed in the previous 24 hours

options.label: C
options.text: oxygen consumption and the respiratory quotient

options.label: D
options.text: carbon dioxide production and the respiratory quotient

questions.why: Indirect calorimetry estimates metabolic rate by measuring O2 consumption and CO2 production.

notes.A: Direct calorimetry, but not the usual estimate.

questions.stem: Carbonic anhydrase has a role to play in the formation of:

options.label: A
options.text: HCl by the parietal cells of the stomach

options.label: C
options.text: cerebrospinal fluid in the choroid plexuses

questions.why: Carbonic anhydrase supplies H+ for the parietal cell proton pump and HCO3- for CSF secretion by the choroid plexus. Carbamino compounds form directly from CO2 and globin amino groups, without the enzyme.

questions.stem: The energy equivalent of oxygen (EEO) is:

options.label: A
options.text: determined by the body temperature and is the same when all the substances are oxidized

options.label: B
options.text: the amount of energy released, when one litre of O2 is utilized for the oxidation of a given substance

options.label: C
options.text: of highest value when lipids are oxidized, since they have the highest calorie content

options.label: D
options.text: the ratio of CO2 produced and O2 utilized

options.label: E
options.text: the energy, expended at rest for 24 hours

questions.why: EEO is the amount of energy released per liter of oxygen consumed.

notes.C: Carbohydrate is highest per litre of O2.
